subject: physics
question_text: Explain how surface tension can be measured experimentally.

mark_split.label: Dip a capillary tube, liquid rises
The relation, with every symbol named
A wetting liquid: cos θ nearly one

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya IPE Study Material for Jr. Students 2026-27 edition, physics volume, Chapter 10 Short Answer Question 13 (printed p.110). Only the question was taken; the answer, its steps and its mark split are original work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. The four-way mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Physics hand-checked: by the capillary rise method, a liquid rises to a height h in a clean capillary tube of radius r dipped vertically into it; at equilibrium the vertical component of the surface tension force around the rim, T cos θ × 2πr, balances the weight of the raised column, πr²hρg, giving T = hrρg/(2 cos θ); for a liquid that wets the glass, θ is nearly zero, cos θ is nearly one, and T = hrρg/2.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: Dip a capillary tube, liquid rises
lines: Dip a clean capillary tube of radius
r vertically into the liquid. The
liquid rises up the tube to a
height h above the free surface
outside the tube.
steps.margin_note: First mark. Name the apparatus: a clean capillary tube of radius r, rising to height h.
steps.why: The tube must be narrow for the rise to be large enough to read, and clean because a film of grease changes the angle of contact.
common_mistakes: Describing an ordinary wide tube. A capillary tube has a narrow bore.
Leaving out that the tube must be clean, which the reading depends on.

recall.must_convey: That a clean capillary tube of radius r is dipped into the liquid, which rises to a height h.
reject: T equals h r rho g by two cos theta

steps.memory_tip: Narrow clean tube, liquid rises to height h.

steps.label: Surface tension force balances weight
lines: At equilibrium, the upward pull of
surface tension around the rim of
the tube balances the weight of the
raised column of liquid:

lines.text: T cos θ × 2πr = πr² h ρ g

steps.margin_note: Second mark. Equate the surface tension force to the weight of the raised column.
steps.why: The liquid stops rising exactly where these two forces balance, so equating them is the whole derivation in one line.
common_mistakes: Leaving out cos θ. The surface tension acts along the tangent to the liquid surface, not straight up.
Using the wrong volume for the raised column instead of the cylinder πr²h.

recall.must_convey: That at equilibrium T cos θ times 2 pi r equals the weight of the raised column, pi r squared h rho g.
accept: T cos theta into two pi r
equals pi r squared h rho g
reject: clean capillary tube of radius r
heard_as: pi r squared h rho g

steps.memory_tip: Tension around the rim holds up the weight of the column.

steps.label: The relation, with every symbol named
steps.mark_note: T = h r ρ g / (2 cos θ)
lines: Dividing both sides by 2πr cos θ,

lines.text: T = h r ρ g / (2 cos θ)

lines: h is the height risen, r the radius
of the tube, ρ the density of the
liquid, θ the angle of contact and
g the acceleration due to gravity.
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Name every symbol: h, r, ρ, θ and g.
steps.why: The formula is only useful once every symbol is tied to a measurable quantity, so naming them is as much a part of the answer as the algebra.
common_mistakes: Writing r as the diameter of the tube. It is the radius.
Leaving one of the five symbols unnamed.

recall.must_convey: That T equals h r rho g divided by two cos theta, with h the height, r the radius, rho the density, theta the angle of contact and g the acceleration due to gravity.
accept: T equals h r rho g by two cos theta
h is the height, r the radius
theta is the angle of contact
reject: T cos theta into two pi r

steps.memory_tip: h, r, ρ, θ, g — every symbol in T = hrρg/(2cos θ) is measurable.

steps.label: A wetting liquid: cos θ nearly one
steps.mark_note: cos θ ≈ 1 for a wetting liquid
lines: For a liquid that wets the glass,
such as water, the angle of contact
θ is nearly zero, so cos θ is
nearly one:
Measuring h for a tube of known
radius r then gives T directly.
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. State θ is nearly zero for a wetting liquid, so cos θ is nearly one.
steps.why: Most liquids used in this experiment wet clean glass, so this simplified form is the one actually used to calculate T from the measured h and r.
common_mistakes: Applying T = hrρg/2 to a liquid that does not wet the tube, such as mercury, where θ is far from zero.
Writing θ as exactly zero rather than nearly zero, which is why cos θ is nearly one, not exactly one.

recall.must_convey: That for a liquid which wets the glass, θ is nearly zero and cos θ is nearly one, so T = h r ρ g / 2.
accept: T equals h r rho g by two
reject: h is the height, r the radius

steps.memory_tip: Wets the glass: θ ≈ 0, cos θ ≈ 1, T = hrρg/2.

insider_note: The formula alone, without naming h, r, ρ, θ and g, reads as a memorised line; naming every symbol is what shows the method is understood.
